results.question: Which influenza virus types cause seasonal epidemics in people in the United States?
results.generated_answer: Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people in the United States almost every winter [1].

chunk.text: There are four types of influenza viruses: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people (known as flu season) almost every winter in the United States. Influenza A viruses are the only influenza viruses known to cause flu pandemics (i.e., global epidemics of flu disease). Influenza C virus infections generally cause mild illness and are not thought to cause human epidemics. Influenza D viruses primarily affect cattle with spillover to other animals but are not known to cause illness in people.

Influenza A viruses are divided into subtypes based on two proteins on the surface of the virus: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). There are 18 hemagglutinin subtypes and 11 neuraminidase subtypes (H1 through H18 and N1 through N11, respectively). Current subtypes of influenza A viruses that routinely circulate in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). Currently circulating influenza A(H1N1) viruses are descendants of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus that emerged in the spring of 2009 and caused a flu pandemic. B/Yamagata viruses have not been detected after March 2020.

Measles is highly contagious. If one person has it, up to 9 out of 10 people who come into close contact with that person will become infected if they are not protected. Measles symptoms appear 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus. Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.

chunk.text: Yellowstone National Park is as wondrous as it is complex. Grand Canyon National Park is a World Heritage Site, encompasses 1,218,375 acres and lies on the Colorado Plateau in northwestern Arizona. Incised by the Colorado River, the canyon is immense, averaging 4,000 feet deep for its entire 277 miles. It is 6,000 feet deep at its deepest point and 18 miles at its widest.

Since the most recent giant (caldera-forming) eruption 631,000 years ago, approximately 80 relatively nonexplosive eruptions have occurred. Of these eruptions, at least 27 were rhyolite lava flows in the caldera, 13 were rhyolite lava flows outside the caldera, and 40 were basalt vents outside the caldera. The most recent volcanic eruption at Yellowstone, a lava flow on the Pitchstone Plateau, occurred 70,000 years ago.

chunk.text: There are four types of influenza viruses: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A viruses are the only influenza viruses known to cause flu pandemics (i.e., global epidemics of flu disease). Influenza C virus infections generally cause mild illness and are not thought to cause human epidemics. Influenza D viruses primarily affect cattle with spillover to other animals but are not known to cause illness in people.

Influenza A viruses are divided into subtypes based on two proteins on the surface of the virus: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). There are 18 hemagglutinin subtypes and 11 neuraminidase subtypes (H1 through H18 and N1 through N11, respectively). Current subtypes of influenza A viruses that routinely circulate in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). Currently circulating influenza A(H1N1) viruses are descendants of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus that emerged in the spring of 2009 and caused a flu pandemic. B/Yamagata viruses have not been detected after March 2020.

chunk.text: Partially piloted manually by Armstrong, the Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility in Site 2 at 0 degrees, 41 minutes, 15 seconds north latitude and 23 degrees, 26 minutes east longitude. This was about four miles downrange from the predicted touchdown point and occurred almost one-and-a-half minutes earlier than scheduled. It included a powered descent that ran a mere nominal 40 seconds longer than preflight planning due to translation maneuvers to avoid a crater during the final phase of landing.

The primary objective of Apollo 11 was to complete a national goal set by President John F. Kennedy on May 25, 1961: perform a crewed lunar landing and return to Earth. Apollo 11 launched from Cape Kennedy on July 16, 1969, carrying Commander Neil Armstrong, Command Module Pilot Michael Collins and Lunar Module Pilot Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin into an initial Earth-orbit of 114 by 116 miles. An estimated 650 million people watched Armstrong's televised image and heard his voice describe the event as he took "one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind" on July 20, 1969.

results.question: Which influenza virus types cause seasonal epidemics in people in the United States?
results.generated_answer: Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people in the United States almost every winter [1].

chunk.text: There are four types of influenza viruses: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people (known as flu season) almost every winter in the United States. Influenza A viruses are the only influenza viruses known to cause flu pandemics (i.e., global epidemics of flu disease). Influenza C virus infections generally cause mild illness and are not thought to cause human epidemics. Influenza D viruses primarily affect cattle with spillover to other animals but are not known to cause illness in people.

Influenza A viruses are divided into subtypes based on two proteins on the surface of the virus: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). There are 18 hemagglutinin subtypes and 11 neuraminidase subtypes (H1 through H18 and N1 through N11, respectively). Current subtypes of influenza A viruses that routinely circulate in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). Currently circulating influenza A(H1N1) viruses are descendants of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus that emerged in the spring of 2009 and caused a flu pandemic. B/Yamagata viruses have not been detected after March 2020.

Measles is highly contagious. If one person has it, up to 9 out of 10 people who come into close contact with that person will become infected if they are not protected. Measles symptoms appear 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus. Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.

results.question: Why was Yellowstone National Park established, and how large is the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem?
results.generated_answer: Yellowstone National Park was established primarily to protect hydrothermal areas that contain about half the world's active geysers [1]. The park forms the core of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, and at 28,000 square miles, it is one of the largest, nearly intact temperate-zone ecosystems on Earth [1].

chunk.text: Yellowstone National Park is as wondrous as it is complex. Established primarily to protect hydrothermal areas that contain about half the world's active geysers, the park also forms the core of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. At 28,000 square miles, it is one of the largest, nearly intact temperate-zone ecosystems on Earth. It preserves a great variety of terrestrial, aquatic, and microbial life.

chunk.text: The most recent volcanic activity at Yellowstone consisted of rhyolitic lava flows that erupted approximately 70,000 years ago. The largest of these flows formed the Pitchstone Plateau in southwestern Yellowstone National Park.

Grand Canyon National Park is a World Heritage Site, encompasses 1,218,375 acres and lies on the Colorado Plateau in northwestern Arizona. Incised by the Colorado River, the canyon is immense, averaging 4,000 feet deep for its entire 277 miles. It is 6,000 feet deep at its deepest point and 18 miles at its widest.

Since the most recent giant (caldera-forming) eruption 631,000 years ago, approximately 80 relatively nonexplosive eruptions have occurred. Of these eruptions, at least 27 were rhyolite lava flows in the caldera, 13 were rhyolite lava flows outside the caldera, and 40 were basalt vents outside the caldera. The most recent volcanic eruption at Yellowstone, a lava flow on the Pitchstone Plateau, occurred 70,000 years ago.

results.question: Which influenza virus types cause seasonal epidemics in people in the United States?
results.generated_answer: Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people in the United States almost every winter [1].

chunk.text: There are four types of influenza viruses: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people (known as flu season) almost every winter in the United States. Influenza A viruses are the only influenza viruses known to cause flu pandemics (i.e., global epidemics of flu disease). Influenza C virus infections generally cause mild illness and are not thought to cause human epidemics. Influenza D viruses primarily affect cattle with spillover to other animals but are not known to cause illness in people.

Influenza A viruses are divided into subtypes based on two proteins on the surface of the virus: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). There are 18 hemagglutinin subtypes and 11 neuraminidase subtypes (H1 through H18 and N1 through N11, respectively). Current subtypes of influenza A viruses that routinely circulate in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). Currently circulating influenza A(H1N1) viruses are descendants of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus that emerged in the spring of 2009 and caused a flu pandemic. B/Yamagata viruses have not been detected after March 2020.

results.question: Which influenza A subtypes routinely circulate in people, and do influenza D viruses cause illness in people?
results.generated_answer: Currently circulating influenza A subtypes in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2) [2]. Influenza D viruses are not known to cause illness in people [1].

chunk.text: There are four types of influenza viruses: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people (known as flu season) almost every winter in the United States. Influenza A viruses are the only influenza viruses known to cause flu pandemics (i.e., global epidemics of flu disease). Influenza C virus infections generally cause mild illness and are not thought to cause human epidemics. Influenza D viruses primarily affect cattle with spillover to other animals but are not known to cause illness in people.

Influenza A viruses are divided into subtypes based on two proteins on the surface of the virus: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). There are 18 hemagglutinin subtypes and 11 neuraminidase subtypes (H1 through H18 and N1 through N11, respectively). Current subtypes of influenza A viruses that routinely circulate in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). Currently circulating influenza A(H1N1) viruses are descendants of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus that emerged in the spring of 2009 and caused a flu pandemic. B/Yamagata viruses have not been detected after March 2020.

Measles is highly contagious. If one person has it, up to 9 out of 10 people who come into close contact with that person will become infected if they are not protected. Measles symptoms appear 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus. Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.

results.question: Which influenza virus types cause seasonal epidemics in people in the United States?

chunk.text: There are four types of influenza viruses: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people (known as flu season) almost every winter in the United States. Influenza A viruses are the only influenza viruses known to cause flu pandemics (i.e., global epidemics of flu disease). Influenza C virus infections generally cause mild illness and are not thought to cause human epidemics. Influenza D viruses primarily affect cattle with spillover to other animals but are not known to cause illness in people.

Influenza A viruses are divided into subtypes based on two proteins on the surface of the virus: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). There are 18 hemagglutinin subtypes and 11 neuraminidase subtypes (H1 through H18 and N1 through N11, respectively). Current subtypes of influenza A viruses that routinely circulate in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). Currently circulating influenza A(H1N1) viruses are descendants of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus that emerged in the spring of 2009 and caused a flu pandemic. B/Yamagata viruses have not been detected after March 2020.

chunk.text: There are four types of influenza viruses: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people (known as flu season) almost every winter in the United States. Influenza A viruses are the only influenza viruses known to cause flu pandemics (i.e., global epidemics of flu disease). Influenza C virus infections generally cause mild illness and are not thought to cause human epidemics. Influenza D viruses primarily affect cattle with spillover to other animals but are not known to cause illness in people.

Influenza A viruses are divided into subtypes based on two proteins on the surface of the virus: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). There are 18 hemagglutinin subtypes and 11 neuraminidase subtypes (H1 through H18 and N1 through N11, respectively). Current subtypes of influenza A viruses that routinely circulate in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). Currently circulating influenza A(H1N1) viruses are descendants of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus that emerged in the spring of 2009 and caused a flu pandemic. B/Yamagata viruses have not been detected after March 2020.

Measles is highly contagious. If one person has it, up to 9 out of 10 people who come into close contact with that person will become infected if they are not protected. Measles symptoms appear 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus. Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.

results.question: Are influenza A viruses the only influenza viruses known to cause flu pandemics?

chunk.text: There are four types of influenza viruses: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics of disease in people (known as flu season) almost every winter in the United States. Influenza A viruses are the only influenza viruses known to cause flu pandemics (i.e., global epidemics of flu disease). Influenza C virus infections generally cause mild illness and are not thought to cause human epidemics. Influenza D viruses primarily affect cattle with spillover to other animals but are not known to cause illness in people.

Influenza A viruses are divided into subtypes based on two proteins on the surface of the virus: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). There are 18 hemagglutinin subtypes and 11 neuraminidase subtypes (H1 through H18 and N1 through N11, respectively). Current subtypes of influenza A viruses that routinely circulate in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). Currently circulating influenza A(H1N1) viruses are descendants of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus that emerged in the spring of 2009 and caused a flu pandemic. B/Yamagata viruses have not been detected after March 2020.

Measles is highly contagious. If one person has it, up to 9 out of 10 people who come into close contact with that person will become infected if they are not protected. Measles symptoms appear 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus. Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.
